analysis.title: "A Tail Of Two Cities": Hartnett Says "Start Adding Some Bonds"
key_insights: Hartnett's two risk-off deleveraging triggers from last week: global financials (IXG) below $125 and MOVE above 125. IXG is just above the line and MOVE hit 110 this week.
The 10Y yield hit 5.33%, the highest since 2002, driven largely by Brent back above $100. Hartnett moved from "nibbling" at bonds to telling clients to "buy humiliation" and start adding some bonds.

YTD scoreboard: oil +61.8%, global stocks +12.1%, US stocks +12.0%, US dollar +3.8%, cash +2.7%, HY bonds -0.3%, IG -3.2%, bitcoin -3.4%, gold -3.8%, govt bonds -4.1%. Gold went from -1.1% to -3.8% YTD and trails cash by 6.5 points.
Q3 winners: bitcoin +43%, oil +42%, software +18%, Mag7 +11%. Q3 losers: zero-coupon bonds -15%, semis -11%, industrials -10%, Korea -8% (Korea still +98% YTD).

Biotech stocks and 10Y yields have both surged in 2026. Hartnett says that combination has appeared only in 1999, 2009 and 2013, and the open question is whether 2026 is a bubbly 1999 or a boomy 2009.

Market breadth is split: 400 SPX stocks are below their 50-day average and 300 are below their 200-day, while the index sits at record highs. Hartnett describes the market as "long artificial intelligence" (NDX) and "short artificial irrelevance" (SPW), with MAG7, AI and biotech unaffected by higher rates and the 1999 analog intact.
Before the March 2000 peak, tech rose more than 40% in six months while staples fell 30% and every sector except tech and telecoms declined. Hartnett uses this as the 1999 template.

Hartnett's view is that it is risk-off until the US dollar peaks. The dollar is spiking on credit event risk, and deleveraging-style price action shows in the Aussie dollar, French bonds, risk parity (RPAR), bond insurers (AGO) and tech CDS (ORCL).

New levels to watch beyond IXG and MOVE: MDY (mid-caps) below $666 and IJR (small-caps) below $135, if they follow banks down. AUD/JPY has rolled over from its June high, Hartnett draws the risk-off line at 110, and it closed just below that on Friday.

Oracle CDS hit record wides and its bonds hit a record low on Sep 25 as its $30 billion capex plan came into question. Its 2056 bonds (Baa2/BBB-) yielded 8% for the first time, above the B2 average of 7.5%. If Oracle is cut to junk, about $120bn of bonds would leave IG indexes.

Hartnett expects policymakers to act as a backstop with open-ended Treasury buybacks and yield-curve control, since the administration is unlikely to let the long end hurt the AI capex boom and stocks into the midterms a month away. This limits the downside unless small and mid-caps and banks break down.

Railroad bubble comparison: every major bubble since (roaring 20s, Nifty Fifty, Japan, internet) peaked at roughly 40% of market cap, but railroads hit 63% in 1881. The AI Big 10 is at 42%, up from 41% last week.

First railroad bubble (ended 1873): stocks tripled 1861-1872, track mileage doubled from 35,000 to 70,000 miles, and capex peaked at about 5% of GDP. The Franco-Prussian war triggered a US credit crunch, Jay Cooke & Company collapsed and about 115 railroads went bankrupt within 12 months.

Second railroad bubble (ended 1881): stocks rose 2.5x from 1877 to 1881 and reached 63% of the US equity market. Construction quadrupled in four years, which crushed freight rates. Construction then fell 42% in 1882, setting off a banking panic, $150mn of gold outflows to Europe and the 1882-85 recession.

AI capex is still below railroad levels: hyperscaler capex of $1.2-1.4 trillion is on track for 3.5-4% of GDP in 2027, below the 5% peaks of the 1870s railroads and the late-1990s fiber buildout. Semiconductor prices are rising, unlike the roughly 5% annual freight rate deflation in the 1870s-80s. Business spending on computers and peripherals has nearly tripled since Q3 2023 to $401bn.

The bad news from the railroad comparison: those booms were backstopped by falling Treasury yields, which is not the case today. Both railroad tops came with credit events, sharp liquidity declines and geopolitics-driven capital outflows.

Hartnett's "buy humiliation" call: negative long-run returns were good entry points for stocks in 1939, 1974 and 2009 and for commodities in 1933 and 2018. Long-run Treasury returns are the worst in 100 years, and ZROZ is down 65% from its March 2020 peak. Ten-year rolling Treasury returns are at -2%.
Hartnett says a 100-200bps fall in yields probably needs a credit event or a recession. He notes asset allocators are very long stocks and very short bonds.

On hyperscaler debt: US IG tech bonds (CITE) are down 9% over the past year, with yield up from 4.5% to 6.2%. Long-term hyperscaler yields are Oracle 8.4%, Meta 7.5% and Google 6.9%. Hartnett argues that because AI is backstopped by the US government, these yields may soon tempt buyers.

Positioning runs the other way: GS Prime Brokerage shows 9 of the 10 most-shorted US IG bonds are long-dated META, NVDA, ORCL, GOOGL and SPCX paper. CoreWeave 9.25% 2030s are the most-shorted HY bond, and Oracle has the largest IG market value on loan.

EPFR flows for the week: $18.8bn to bonds, $15.8bn to stocks, $0.9bn to crypto, $0.7bn to gold, and $118.0bn out of cash on quarter-end. Long-term bonds took $7.4bn (largest since May 2025), municipal bonds $4.2bn (largest ever), Europe equities $1.3bn, China equities $3.7bn, tech $3.3bn and utilities $1.0bn.
Money-market funds lost 1.1% of AUM in the quarter-end shuffle. BofA private clients hold a record 66.3% of assets in stocks and a record-low 9.4% in cash.

The BofA Bull & Bear Indicator fell to 8.8 from 9.3, due to wider spreads in risky bonds, HY bond outflows and deteriorating global breadth. A net 27% of global equity indices trade below both their 50- and 200-day averages, the worst since March. At 8.8 it remains in "sell" territory.

The author's bottom line: in both railroad busts the trigger was credit, liquidity and capital leaving abroad, and the same three are showing in Oracle CDS, AUD/JPY and French bonds. If small caps follow banks lower, Hartnett's own playbook says the risk-off cascade is here regardless of the policy put.

tension_points.bull_case: Hartnett says to buy bonds. Long-run Treasury returns are the worst in 100 years, allocators are very short bonds, and policy backstops (buybacks, YCC) will cap yields before the midterms.
tension_points.bear_case: The 10Y at 5.33% with Brent above $100 is the cost-of-money pressure that ended both railroad bubbles. Credit, liquidity and capital outflow signals are already showing in Oracle CDS, AUD/JPY and French bonds.
tension_points.what_invalidates: IXG below $125, MOVE above 125, or MDY below $666 and IJR below $135 would signal the risk-off cascade.

tension_points.bull_case: Hyperscaler bond yields (Oracle 8.4%, Meta 7.5%, Google 6.9%) may tempt buyers because the US government backstops AI.
tension_points.bear_case: Oracle CDS is at record wides and the bonds yield above the B2 average, with about $120bn at risk of leaving IG indexes if Oracle is cut to junk. Nine of the 10 most-shorted US IG bonds are hyperscaler paper.
tension_points.what_invalidates: An Oracle downgrade to junk would force about $120bn of bonds out of IG indexes.
